narrative:
The model predicted a 64% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your third-year class ranking had the strongest influence, followed by your LSAT score, then your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your first-year and third-year deciles placed you at the very bottom of your class (decile 1), far below the average of roughly 6 among students who were accepted. These unusually low academic rankings signaled to the model a high risk of struggling with the bar exam. Your LSAT score of 19 was also substantially below the 37-point average of accepted students, reinforcing the same concern about readiness for the exam. Together, these academic signals outweighed other details such as your middle-income background, part-time study plans, gender, and race (which the model did not consider).

To improve your chances, focus on raising your academic performance and retaking the LSAT to reach at least the mid-30s. Strengthening these two areas would most directly reduce your predicted risk of failing the bar exam. Consider targeted test preparation or additional coursework before reapplying.
